Chapter 1 — Five Feet from the Fire

The phone started its angry little dance at 2:17 a.m., skittering across the oak nightstand until it hit the lamp with a dull clack. Jasper Barrett was already half out of bed by the second buzz, hand closing around the phone, feet finding the floor like the room had tilted and the only way to keep balance was forward.



URGENT: SYSTEMS COMPROMISE — EUROPE. NEED YOU LIVE.



He didn’t curse. Didn’t sigh. He stood, shouldered the thin ache that lived between his shoulder blades, and reached for the leather go-bag hanging off the closet knob. Zipper check, charger coil, two suits, one pair of running shoes, passport wallet. The ritual steadied his hands.



Beside him, Elena rolled toward the sound. “Work?”



“Yeah.” Jasper kept his voice low, the room’s blue-dark swallowing most of it. “Big one.”



“Of course it is.” No bite—just the soft resignation of someone who’d learned how to fold sleeplessness into her bones and carry it like it weighed less than it did.



Down the hall, a nightlight cast a pale square on the carpet outside Grace’s room. He did a quick calculus: twelve seconds to step in, kiss her forehead, risk waking her and starting the day’s anxiety eight hours early—or zero seconds, let her sleep, and be the surprise at breakfast if breakfast happened. Five feet at a time. He stayed in the hall.



Shower. Heat woke muscle. He let the water drum his neck and mentally cleared the board: unknown entry vector; client’s European hub; potential data loss; regulatory clocks already whispering to life in three countries; press timers ticking in six. A dozen branching paths, none yet paved. Five feet, he told himself. Don’t write the statement before you know what it needs to say.



He dressed fast—dark suit, white shirt open at the throat, tie shoved into the go-bag. In the kitchen, he dropped the laptop on the counter next to the coffee machine and opened three windows: an encrypted chat with his team, a sandboxed browser, a clean document for the timeline. The machine hissed, the room filling with the smell of ground beans and the ghost of yesterday’s toast. His phone lit. Addison.



He answered on speaker, typing as he spoke. “Tell me what we actually know.”



“Six minutes ago, Frankfurt ops reported a critical systems fail,” Addison Price said, voice smooth as glass and twice as hard. “Network access spiked from an unrecognized admin credential chained through a vendor VPN. Their SOC killed the session. We don’t know what they took.”



“Who knows?”



“CIO, CISO, CTO. CEO is ‘on his way.’” Addison made air quotes with her tone. “Local comms head is already drafting nonsense.”



“Kill any drafts,” Jasper said. “Nothing goes out that isn’t water‑tight. Put Legal and Privacy on a separate line. I want a clean log of actions since detection.”



A second ringtone bled into the call—London security. He merged them.



“Don’t tell me what you think,” he said by way of greeting. “Tell me what you can swear to under oath.”



Frankfurt’s head of security sounded like a man juggling knives. “Third-party credential abuse. Thirty-one minutes between first anomalous activity and kill. We’ve isolated the vendor tunnel and revoked. Forensics are imaging. We… don’t have a confirmed exfil.”



“Any evidence of lateral movement pre-credential?”



A beat. “We’re still—”



“Looking,” Jasper finished for him. “Fine. Stand up a shadow environment. Get me a copy of access logs for the last ninety days, scoped to elevated roles. And call their vendor’s CISO. Not the account rep. I want the fish, not the bait.”



He ended the merge, left Addison on. “Spin up the war room,” he said. “London time. Twelve seats. Screens up, mics hot, sentiment tracker on the big board. I’ll be airborne in ninety.”



“You’re not driving yourself, are you?” Addison asked, already clicking.



“Car in five,” he said, though he hadn’t called one yet. She knew him well enough to assume the next five feet were done before he named them.



Elena stepped into the doorway, robe knotted tight. Hair pulled back, eyes heavy. She watched him pack the laptop, the way his hands moved like there was a metronome set somewhere inside his chest.



“You’ll call?” she asked.



“From the plane,” he said. “And when I land.”



The corner of her mouth did something small—skepticism softened by muscle memory. He crossed to her and kissed her temple, catching the warmth of skin that still felt like home even when he wasn’t there enough to earn the word. “Tell Grace I love her.”



“You tell her,” Elena said. “Tomorrow.”



He nodded. Promises were lighter at two a.m. They weighed what they weighed in daylight.



Outside, the rideshare idled at the curb, exhaust ghosting the air. The city felt hollowed out at this hour—streetlights, a late bus grumbling, a fox darting across a yard like a rumor. Jasper slid into the back seat and dialed the client CEO.



“Barrett,” the man barked when he picked up, impatient terror in the back of his throat. “What’s happening? Do we need to go public?”



“Not yet,” Jasper said, watching sodium-hazed blocks stream by. “If you talk without facts, you create the story. We need timeline, scope, and chain-of-custody. Anything else is noise.”



“Share price—”



“Will survive a smart twenty-four hours,” Jasper cut him off. “It won’t survive a sloppy two.”



Silence. Surrender, or at least the holding pattern he could turn into surrender. He ended the call and texted his deputy: Build three trees. One: contained, no PII. Two: limited PII, proactive notification. Three: worst-case. Draft statements that say nothing and sound like something. Placeholders for quotes only.**



The driver took the ramp to the highway and the city unspooled. Jasper let his head rest against the glass, the cool a brief mercy. Reflex pressed a thumb to his watch, a habit Elena loved and hated for what it gave away—thoughts moving too fast for words. He took his hand away and opened Grace’s last text instead: a photo of a paper lighthouse on the kitchen table, door cut with blunt scissors, colored pencil beam of light sweeping a construction-paper sea. I made this in art she’d written, followed by three lighthouse emojis and a single crooked heart.



He swallowed. Set the phone face down. Five feet.



At the airport, security felt like muscle memory: ID, trays, belt, shoes, the whole mechanical humility of people who want their day back. He hated airports less than he pretended. They were clean boxes with clear rules and predictable outcomes. You walked in one person and walked out in another city. Transformation by moving walkway.



He hit the lounge for ten minutes of power and quiet and called home. Elena answered on the second ring.



“You at the gate?” she asked.



“Boarding soon.” He listened, and the tiny sounds came through—the kettle boiling, the whisper of her socked feet on tile. “You should sleep.”



“I will.” She didn’t. They both knew it. “Jas?”



“Yeah.”



“Bring yourself back. Not just your suitcase.”



He exhaled. “I will.”



He almost said I’ll make it up to you. He didn’t. He’d retired that lie.



On the plane, he took an aisle and opened the laptop before the flight attendant finished her safety pantomime. He built the timeline at speed: 01:46 CET first anomaly; 02:17 admin credential spike; 02:34 vendor tunnel revoked; 02:47 Jasper looped in; 03:03 war room live. He checked the sentiment monitor—grey and green. No red yet. Good. He wrote the first line of the holding statement in his head and deleted it before his fingers could type it. Never lead with regret. Lead with posture.



Somewhere over the Atlantic, turbulence trembled the metal and the cabin lit with the blue ghost of seatback screens. Jasper’s eyes closed, not asleep—just a quick blackout his body took without asking. When he opened them, he saw the version of himself reflected faintly in the dark window: jaw tight, tie abandoned, pupils pinpricks from the laptop burn. The man looked like he could break a room open with a paragraph. He also looked like he hadn’t learned to sit still in years.



He flipped the passport wallet open to check landing forms and found the photo he always forgot he’d put there. Elena on the beach, wind in her hair, Grace a toddler at her hip, a kite string cutting the sky into triangles. The picture had been printed at a pharmacy and handled too much—colors softened into the suggestion of sky and skin. He let his thumb rest on the edge. Not long. Just long enough to feel paper and remember that it wasn’t the same as being there.



He tucked it back and wrote the questions a good reporter would ask. Then he wrote the answers the company could survive saying out loud. He built a matrix of what to give regulators, what to hold, what to say only once under tight privilege. The work turned noisy thought into clean lines. The muscles in his shoulders unwound by degrees.



When they landed, London’s morning was a pale bruise. He stepped into the clean chill and moved the way he always moved in a new time zone: like the clock was a thing he could outpace.



The client’s glass tower housed a war room on the twenty-third floor—the kind of space that wanted you to feel like crises were solvable if you had enough screens. His team was already there: Mac bent over a laptop, dark eyes flicking between log extracts and a graph he’d built; Rina on a call with vendors, her voice the kind of polite that made grown men confess; Lexi at the whiteboard, jotting verbs that sounded like action without implying blame yet; Addison at the head of the table, immaculate and bulletproof, the gravity that kept the orbits stable.



Jasper dropped his bag, rolled his sleeves, and started talking before anyone could remember to stand. “We run three tracks. Containment, compliance, comms. If anyone crosses lanes, I cut your hands off. Legal, privilege wrapper is in effect—no one says ‘hack’ unless they’re quoting someone else. Mac, show me the heat map.”



Mac tapped two keys; the big screen bloomed with color—green systems, yellow for touch points, angry red pulsing along a path that made Jasper’s mouth go flat.



“Vendor tunnel gave them jump‑off into legacy middleware,” Mac said. “No confirmed exfil, but if they touched this, they could’ve seen the table of keys.”



“Could have is not did,” Jasper said. “We don’t chase ghosts in public. Rina?”



“Vendor CISO is on,” she said, sliding a headset down and pushing a new feed to the screen. “They’re claiming MFA. Logs say otherwise.”



“Of course,” Jasper muttered. “Put them in the corner until they remember what ‘cooperate’ means. Lexi, three drafts on my desk in twenty: ‘containment confirmed,’ ‘containment in progress,’ ‘containment inconclusive.’ No adjectives. Verbs carry load. We’re not soothing—we’re telling the truth with its sharp edges rounded so no one bleeds by accident.”



Lexi’s eyes flicked up. “You want empathy line?”



“Two,” Jasper said. “For customers and for staff. The public forgets staff are the public.”



Addison watched him with that impenetrable calm that made CEOs defer without knowing why. “Barrett,” she said, low enough to be just between them. “You sleeping?”



“On planes,” he said.



“Not the same,” she said.



“Close enough today.”



She didn’t argue. She nodded at the room. “He has it. Do it his way.”



The next hour broke into action—calls, logs, lines. The red on the big screen cooled pink, then grey as teams isolated segments and unplugged what didn’t need to hum. Jasper moved through it with the clean economy of motion he used when running a line tight enough to hold a man over a ledge. Five feet. This, then that. Don’t care about the river; care about the next stone.



His phone buzzed in his pocket. Two short, one long—Elena’s pattern. He let it vibrate. He would call on a break. He would make a break. He wrote “CALL HOME” at the bottom corner of the glass with a small, decisive square next to it, like if he could just give the need a checkbox, he’d honor it.



He finished a sentence for the CEO—“We will not speculate”—and drew a circle around the words. A breath he hadn’t realized he’d been holding eased out. The room exhaled with him. Screens quieted to the soft chatter of clean systems.



“Scenario one,” he told Lexi. “Containment confirmed. Keep it narrow. Give them one sentence they can repeat without lying.”



She nodded, already writing. “What about the rumor mill?”



“Starve it,” he said. “No oxygen.”



“Street wants a mea culpa,” someone from Legal said from the back, voice edged.

“Hey,” he said, and for a moment the steady, controlled cadence he used to talk men with microphones away from cliffs faded. He sounded like himself, or the self he remembered. “It’s contained. I’m coming back tonight.”

“She’ll save you three,” Elena said, a smile ghosting through the line. “Bring yourself back, Jasper.”

FLIGHT. DINNER. YOURSELF.

Chapter 3 — The Call from Home

The first ping came while Jasper was walking Grace to the bus stop. The morning air was clean, crisp enough to taste, the kind that made him think about runs he’d never take. “Not confirmed. But they’re diverting ambulances. CEO’s in a panic. I’ve already got half the team spinning up.”



He looked down the street, watched the bus turn the corner. He’d promised Elena—promised himself—he’d give them a day before disappearing again. “Give me ten minutes,” he said.

“You said that last time.”

She came closer, close enough he could smell the faint citrus from her shampoo. “I don’t want to fight you about the job,” she said quietly. “I just want to be in the part of your life that matters most.”

The car arrived before he could answer.



The command center for the hospital crisis was a converted conference room in a Boston high-rise, wall-to-wall screens glowing with patient load maps, firewall logs, and the creeping red overlay of infected systems. Addison was already on site, headset in place, eyes scanning like a sniper.

“Tell them to scream quieter. Rina—set up a clean shadow scheduler. Get it ready to go live in under two hours. Mac—map ingress and egress. I want the exact infection vector, yesterday.”



The work came fast, his brain locking into the same hyperfocused state it always did. The hum of urgency, the satisfaction of pieces falling into place—it was addictive. Too addictive.



But in the middle of it, his phone buzzed in his pocket. He almost ignored it, then saw the name.



Elena.



“Go,” Addison said, not looking up.

Silence. Then: “Of course you can’t.”

The line went dead.

He nodded, but his eyes were on his phone, on the photo of Grace at the beach that Elena had sent years ago—the one he still carried in his passport wallet.



It didn’t feel like saving.

Flashback — 2011

Not of failing the job.

Of failing her.

Chapter 6 — Project Wildcard

Grace’s drawing lay centered on Jasper’s desk like a paper compass: two capes, one small, one tall, standing shoulder to shoulder. He’d flattened the creases with his palm before the morning stand‑up, told himself he’d leave it there until the project wrapped. A talisman. Or a guardrail.



Addison’s meeting started at 08:00 on the dot. Conference room glass, twelve chairs, and the muted glow of too many screens.



“New intake,” she said, sliding a thin folder across the table to him. “High profile. High velocity. Politically sensitive.”



“Of course it is,” Lexi murmured, twirling a pen. She clocked the crayon drawing as she took her seat and gave Jasper a look that said both cute and you’re going to need it.



Rina popped in on speaker from a tarmac somewhere. “I’ll be remote for the next three hours. Vendor audit at ten.”



Addison tapped the folder. “Private aerospace. Near‑miss at a desert proving ground. A video leaked—unconfirmed telemetry, lots of smoke, very little light. The company’s claiming anomaly in a third‑party component. Regulators are circling, the Hill is sniffing, and the stock’s already sliding.”



“Who’s in the blast radius?” Jasper asked.



“Investors, contractors, and about six agencies that would prefer this embarrassment stayed off the evening news.” Addison’s tone was wry; her eyes weren’t. “We’re lead. We’ll run a tight lane discipline. No freelancing.”



A soft knock at the glass door. Addison didn’t look up. “Come in.”



Harper Vance stepped inside like the room had been arranged to welcome her. Dark hair pulled back, tailored blazer, expression composed to the exact degree that suggested she’d already read the room and decided which corners mattered. She set a tablet on the table, met Jasper’s eyes once—steady, unblinking—and offered a hand.



“Harper Vance. Brought in on specialty.”



Specialty was industry shorthand for the client asked for someone sharp enough to cut the problem open without bleeding out themselves. Her grip was warm, precise. Ana de Armas’s kind of poise—cool on the surface, velocity underneath.



Addison made the introductions without commentary. Jasper noticed that Addison didn’t over‑explain Harper. That was its own kind of introduction.



Harper glanced at the whiteboard, at the bullet points Lexi had sketched while listening. “Who wrote ‘don’t borrow culpability’?” she asked.



“Me,” Jasper said.



“Good line.” She slid into a chair across from him. “Let’s not.”



She launched into a crisp download: the grainy clip, the timing, the way a single unsourced TikTok had metastasized into three think‑pieces and a cable chyron. She spoke in clean angles, cutting away drama until the shape of the crisis emerged. Jasper felt the pull he hadn’t wanted to admit he missed—the hum of a professional operating at his speed.



“We need four tracks,” Harper finished. “Telemetry truth, supply‑chain truth, regulator posture, and a calm public frame that acknowledges risk without feeding hysteria.”



Jasper nodded once. “We’ll run three—and fold your telemetry into Mac’s risk tree.” He didn’t have to look to know Mac had already drafted one. “We keep supply chain and regulator on separate circuits until we’re sure their incentives don’t clash.”



Harper’s mouth curved, not quite a smile. “You’re worried the regulator wants a headline.”



“I’m worried everyone wants a headline,” he said. “We want facts.”



Addison split assignments with surgical efficiency. “Lexi, build three statements: anomaly under review, anomaly isolated, anomaly disproved. No adjectives. Rina, lock vendor intake. Mac, telemetry grid. Harper—ride point on the client CTO. Jasper… you’re on overall.”



He felt Lexi’s quick glance: Overall meant sleep became theoretical. He set Grace’s drawing on the corner of his legal pad where he could feel its weight against his wrist.



The room broke into motion. Harper didn’t; she pivoted toward Jasper instead. “Quick sync?” she asked, already standing.



They stepped into the corridor where the carpet ate sound. Harper kept her voice low. “I’ll need your cover to push their CTO. He’s defensive and two coffee cups past reasonable. He’ll try to own the timeline with vagueness.”



“Then don’t let him,” Jasper said.



“I can do adversarial,” she replied, deadpan. “But it works better if I’m adversarial with a badge.”



“You’ll have it.” He paused. “No hero laps.”



“Not my sport,” she said. For the first time, something like warmth edged her tone. “I’ve read your work. You draw clean boxes. People breathe better in them.”



“Boxes keep people alive,” he said. “And employed.”



“And honest,” she added. The corner of her mouth tipped. “Some of them.”



They moved back in. Lexi intercepted Jasper with a draft on her tablet. “Statement A: ‘We’ve initiated a comprehensive review with independent experts and relevant authorities. Our preliminary analysis indicates the event was contained to a single test article with no injuries. We’ll share verified findings as soon as they’re available.’”



“Lose ‘comprehensive’,” Jasper said. “It’s a tell.”



“Replacing with ‘independent’ alone makes lawyers twitch,” Lexi warned.



“Let them twitch. They’ll live.” He handed the tablet back. “And cut ‘as soon as’—we’re not promising pace we can’t control.”



She grinned. “You’re no fun.” Then, softer, eyes flicking to the drawing, “Good anchor.”



He shrugged. “Trying things.”



“Try keeping it,” she said, and flowed back into the current of the room.



By late morning, the skeleton of control was up: a clean intake channel, a draft Q&A that admitted unknowns without sounding evasive, a decision tree with three exits no one would like but everyone could walk through. The CTO, predictably, bristled at Harper until she sliced his qualifiers into parts and arranged them on the table like evidence.



“Say the verb,” she told him, voice calm enough to be dangerous. “Did the system fail or did it misread?”



He hedged. She waited. Jasper watched the room lean toward her stillness the way frightened people lean toward certainty. He felt the ghost of an old engine turn over in his chest.



At noon, Addison called a fifteen‑minute break. People scattered for coffee and sunlight like divers surfacing. Jasper stayed. Harper stayed too, studying the telemetry freeze frame on the main screen as if it might confess if she stared long enough.



She nodded at the crayon capes on his desk when they were alone. “Good reminder.”



He followed her gaze. “My daughter.”



“How old?”



“Ten. On crutches. Soccer season’s looking… different.” He wasn’t in the habit of offering his life to colleagues; the words surprised him as he heard them.



Harper didn’t fill the silence with sympathetic noise. “I grew up on ski teams,” she said after a beat. “Breaking the season feels like the end of the world. It never is.” Her eyes flicked to him. “As long as the world remembers to show up.”



He felt that land where it was meant to. “Working on it.”



Her phone buzzed. She glanced, grimaced, tucked it away. “CTO’s sending me a log dump with half the useful columns stripped out.”



“Then he sends the other half or we do the press without him.” Jasper’s tone flattened. “Sometimes fear needs leverage.”



“Permission to apply pressure,” she said.



“Permission granted.”



“Copy,” she replied, military‑clean, then added, almost as an aside, “You say ‘we’ like you mean it.”



“I do.”



“Keep it that way,” she said, and left him with the telemetry and his own reflection on the screen—sleeves rolled, tie abandoned, the look of a man standing exactly in the middle of what he’s good at and what might break him.



His phone buzzed. Elena.



He answered before the second ring. “Hey.”



“We got the school schedule for next week,” she said, no preamble. “Grace has PT on Tuesday at four. They asked if a parent could be there to learn the exercises.”



“I’ll be there,” he said.



A pause. “You sure?”



“I’m writing it on the board,” he said, and with the phone still to his ear, he picked up the marker and wrote TUE 4: PT — BE THERE beneath the crisis timeline, a box around it like any other non‑negotiable deliverable. “It’s on mission critical.”



Something in her exhale loosened. “Okay.” Then, softer: “How’s the… rocket thing?”



“Messy,” he said. “Getting cleaner.”



“Try not to blow up on my kitchen counter,” she said, and he could hear the smile she wasn’t ready to give him in person. “We’ll save you a spot on the couch tonight.”



“Hold it for me,” he said.



“I always do,” she replied, and hung up before the sentiment could scare either of them.



When he put the phone down, Harper was at the doorway again, tablet in hand. “CTO folded. Full logs incoming. Also, the Hill wants a briefing ‘off the record’ that will be mysteriously on the record in twenty minutes.”



“Lexi’ll babysit Hill,” Jasper said. “We brief with verbs and remove all adjectives. If anyone insists on adjectives, we use theirs, not ours.”



“Copy,” Harper said, then glanced at the fresh block letters on the edge of the whiteboard. “PT?”



“Physical therapy.” He capped the marker. “Non‑negotiable.”



A line appeared between her brows—respect, not curiosity. “Good box.”



The afternoon accelerated. The telemetry told a story that wasn’t catastrophic, just humanly flawed: a sensor miscalibration compounded by a vendor tolerance no one had audited since a reorg. Not sabotage. Not systemic rot. Fixable, if you were willing to say the unglamorous truth out loud.



Jasper and Lexi built the spine of the statement together—facts first, accountability framed as action not apology. Addison loaded the briefing deck like a contractor checking joists. Harper kept the CTO from gilding or erasing. Mac drew arrows between systems until the room could see how the mistake had happened without turning it into a morality play.



At 17:30, Jasper read the line they’d all been orbiting: “We identified a calibration error in a test article sensor chain and have corrected the tolerance in coordination with our suppliers. We are briefing regulators with our findings and will publish the audited results.”



“Clean,” Addison said.



“Unsexy,” Lexi added.



“True,” Harper finished, and the tiny approval in her voice landed like a note struck true.



They pushed the statement at 18:05. The market didn’t clap, but it stopped bleeding. Reporters grumbled about the lack of adjectives and ran the facts anyway. The Hill’s aide rephrased “calibration error” as “a non‑safety‑critical test anomaly,” and Lexi let it pass with the kind of grace that comes from picking the right battles.



At 18:40, Jasper powered down his screen. The room was still busy; the crisis wasn’t over. But the line had been drawn, and the fire that had started the day had been reduced to heat you could stand next to without blistering.



He slid Grace’s drawing back into his bag. Harper caught the movement.



“Dinner,” she said, not a question.



“PT,” he corrected. “Dinner after.”



She nodded like he’d given the only right answer. “See you at 07:00.”



“08:00,” he said, tapping the block letters he’d written. “Non‑negotiable.”



A glint—amusement, maybe respect—flickered in her eyes. “08:00 it is.”



In the elevator, Lexi leaned against the rail, studying him. “You look… different.”



“Older?” he offered.



“Less haunted,” she said. Then, with a tilt of her chin toward the bag, “Keep the cape handy.”



He stepped out into evening—the city smelling like warm concrete and resolved weather. Traffic moved in its own slow logic. He texted Elena: On my way. Save me a crutch and a couch.



Her reply came fast: We saved your spot. Hurry.



He did. And for once, the distance between the rooms where he was necessary and the rooms where he was needed didn’t feel impossible. The boxes he’d drawn today held. One of them had a ten‑year‑old’s handwriting under it.



He put the car in gear and drove toward home.

Chapter 8 — Fracture Lines

The email subject line was blunt:



Wildcard: Urgent — CEO Request

And then there was the client herself: Alexandra Pierce, mid-forties, composed in that way that made you think nothing could shake her. She asked Jasper three direct questions, eyes fixed on him like he was the only one in the room who mattered.



He answered cleanly, but the way she listened—like she was reading him—was unsettling. He caught himself noticing the shape of her voice, low and certain, before shoving that thought aside.



After the meeting, Harper caught him in the hallway. “She likes you.”

Chapter 9 — When the Floor Gives Way

The house was quiet in that heavy way it only got when Grace was at Aunt Sara’s.

Jasper had come home early for once, still riding the mental edge of the Wildcard meetings, laptop under his arm.



Elena was in the kitchen, barefoot, her hair pulled into a loose braid. She was rinsing out a coffee mug when she swayed a little, like she’d just lost her balance.



“You okay?” he asked.

“Stay with me,” he said, voice breaking as he shifted her carefully onto her side. He grabbed his phone, hands slick with adrenaline, and punched in 911.



“This is Jasper Barrett—my wife just collapsed, she’s not responding—breathing but barely—”

“Follow us to St. Catherine’s,” one of them said.

Chapter 10 — The Line in the Floor

The waiting room at St. Catherine’s smelled like stale coffee and antiseptic. Jasper sat hunched in a molded plastic chair, elbows on his knees, phone in his hands but not moving.

Jasper swallowed hard, pressing the heel of his hand to his eyes until the image broke apart.



That wasn’t real. This was. Elena behind those doors, pale and still. Grace at Sara’s, thinking Mom and Dad were fine.



He glanced at the wall clock. Twenty minutes had passed. Or maybe two hours. Time was elastic here, stretching and snapping in uneven bursts.



The doctor finally appeared — tall, calm, a clipboard tucked under one arm.



“She’s stable,” he said before Jasper could ask. “We’re running more tests, but right now it looks like a severe drop in blood pressure combined with dehydration. It’s good you got her help quickly.”



Relief slammed through him, leaving him weak. “Can I see her?”



“In a few minutes. She’s resting.”



When the doctor left, Jasper pulled his phone back out. This time he didn’t open Harper’s text. He scrolled instead to Grace’s contact.



“Hey, kiddo,” he said when she answered. “Mom’s okay. She just got a little sick, but the doctors are taking care of her. You and Aunt Sara good for the night?”



“We’re fine,” Grace said, but her voice was small. “You’re staying with Mom, right?”



“Yeah,” he said, and meant it in more ways than she could know. “I’m not going anywhere.”



He ended the call and sat back. The hum of the hospital seemed to dull around him.



The Asia trip loomed in his mind — fourteen days of boardrooms, press conferences, and crisis rooms in three countries. It had been locked for weeks. No one would blame him for going.



But in the hollow space the last few hours had carved out of him, the decision felt simple.



He’d tell Harper tomorrow: Wildcard would have to send someone else.



The storms could rage without him.



He was going to be here when Elena opened her eyes.

Chapter 11 — Convergence

Elena leaned her head back against the pillows, watching it all unfold.

“Popular guy,” she murmured.



“Not the kind I want to be,” Jasper said, his hand still on hers.



He looked at each of them — Harper with her efficient competence, Alexandra with her poised detachment, Jessica with her guiding steadiness, and the project colleague with her earnest smile — and realized none of them belonged here the way Elena did.



“I appreciate all of you coming,” he said, “but right now… I just need to be here. With my wife.”



Something shifted in the air then — Harper nodding curtly, Alexandra’s gaze softening for the first time, Jessica giving him a small approving smile.



One by one, they left.



When the room was quiet again, Elena studied him for a long moment.

“You mean it? About not going to Asia?”



“I’m done trying to be everywhere for everyone,” he said. “From now on, I’m going to be here for us.”



Her fingers curled around his. “Then maybe this was the wake-up call we needed.”

Flashback Scene – “While the Building Was Burning”

Eight Years Ago – Midtown Manhattan

The air in the half-finished hotel lobby smelled like plaster dust and stale coffee. Workers shouted over the whine of power tools, their voices carrying a sharp edge — everyone knew this project was weeks behind and bleeding money.



Jessica Vaughn stepped through the sliding glass doors in her tailored charcoal suit, heels clicking against the subfloor. The foreman trailed behind, rattling off excuses about weather delays, supply chain issues, union disputes.



She’d heard it all before.



She was here on behalf of the investors — not to save the job, but to assess whether they should pull the plug. It was supposed to be a two-hour walk-through, a quick diagnosis before she wrote her report.



Halfway through the lobby, she stopped.



At the far end of the room, a man in rolled-up sleeves and a dusty button-down stood at a folding table covered in blueprints, delivery schedules, and Post-its. A phone was wedged between his ear and shoulder as he pointed at a section of ductwork overhead.



“No, you can’t push that to next week,” he said into the phone, voice low but firm. “If you do, we lose the drywall crew. If we lose them, your team is sitting here for two weeks unpaid. You want that?”



A pause. Then: “Good. Truck’s here tomorrow at 7.” He hung up, grabbed a red Sharpie, and marked the blueprint before turning to wave two electricians over.



Jessica (aside to the foreman):

“Who’s that?”



The foreman sighed. “Jasper Barrett. Junior PM. Technically not even supposed to be running point, but…” He gestured to the chaos around them. “…he’s the only one keeping this thing from falling apart.”



Jessica watched him work. In less than five minutes, he’d pulled three trades together, negotiated a delivery, and shifted an inspection window — without raising his voice.



She approached the table.

“You’re not on the meeting schedule,” she said.



He looked up, caught off guard. “Because I’m not in charge.”



“Could’ve fooled me.”



Five Minutes Later

She found herself leaning against the table, listening as he explained the real problems: wrong sequencing on the MEP install, the elevator shaft out of tolerance, imported tile stuck in customs. No jargon, no ego — just clear, rapid-fire solutions.



Finally, she said, “You’re not just putting out fires. You’re redesigning the building while it’s burning down.”



He smirked. “Someone’s gotta.”



By the end of her site visit, Jessica’s report had changed. Instead of recommending a shutdown, she advised giving the project one last chance — with Jasper as the de facto lead.



She didn’t tell the investors the real reason.

She wanted to see what he could do when the leash was off.

Flashback Scene – “While the Building Was Burning”

Eight Years Ago – Uptown Charlotte

The gutted hotel smelled like sawdust, paint thinner, and desperation. Plastic sheeting hung from the ceilings, flapping whenever a worker carried a load of drywall through.



Jessica Vaughn stepped through the propped-open side door, heels tapping against the raw concrete floor. She was here on behalf of the investment group that had sunk millions into the renovation. At a folding table covered in half-curled blueprints and paper coffee cups, a man in a wrinkled button-down with rolled sleeves was juggling three things at once:



A phone wedged under his ear.



A Sharpie in his right hand, marking up ductwork plans.



His left hand gesturing sharply toward two steelworkers arguing over measurements.



“No, you can’t bump it to Monday,” he said into the phone, calm but with that steel edge. “If you do, the millwork guys lose their spot and we lose two weeks. You want that on your bill?”



A pause. Then: “Good. Truck’s here at 6.” He hung up, waved the steelworkers over, and started reassigning tasks without a raised voice.



Jessica leaned toward the foreman.

“Who is that?”



“Jasper Barrett,” the foreman said with a half-smile. “Not even the lead PM. Technically, he’s here to ‘support’ the guy in charge… but he’s the only one keeping this from turning into a lawsuit.”



She watched for five more minutes. He wasn’t just managing — he was triaging. Fixing today’s fire while pulling next week’s schedule into alignment. Talking to contractors like he’d worked every one of their jobs.



She stepped up to his table. “You’re not on my meeting schedule.”



He looked up, a little startled. “Because I’m not in charge.”



“Could’ve fooled me.”



Five minutes later, she was leaning against his table while he explained the mess — HVAC installs out of order, imported fixtures stuck in port, the concrete pour in the parking garage already curing wrong. His breakdown was precise, his solutions fast, and he didn’t waste a single word trying to impress her.



Finally, she said, “You’re not just putting out fires. You’re redesigning the building while it’s burning down.”



He smirked. “Someone’s gotta.”



When she filed her report to the investors that week, she didn’t recommend pulling out.

She recommended one last push — but only if Jasper Barrett ran point.



She didn’t tell them the real reason. She just wanted to see what happened when the leash came off.

Final Chapter – After the Last Glass

The last car pulled away down the gravel drive, its taillights swallowed by the dark Carolina night. The garden tent stood half-empty, flickering string lights swaying in the breeze.



Inside, Elena kicked off her heels with a sigh, dropping them beside the couch. Jasper loosened his tie and poured the last two fingers of whiskey from the decanter into a single glass.

He kissed her forehead, but she caught his jaw and lifted her lips to his. It wasn’t hurried; it was slow, deliberate, like she was claiming something they’d both fought to keep.



When she whispered, “Full clearance, remember?” he chuckled against her mouth.

Hours Later



They made their way upstairs, laughter low in the dark hallway. Clothes trailed behind them like breadcrumbs, and the moonlight through the window cut across their tangled silhouettes. The intimacy was not rushed — it was rediscovery. Every touch felt like stitching a seam that had been frayed for too long.



Morning Light



The smell of coffee drifted in from the kitchen. Elena, hair in a loose knot, was stacking plates from the kitchen counter, moving slower than usual. Jasper stood barefoot at the sink, rinsing out the champagne flutes.



“You know,” she said, “we could’ve hired someone to do all this.”



“And miss the fun of waking up next to you and cleaning up together?” he teased.

He laughed, drying his hands. “I’ll take my chances.”



Closing

He stared at the screen for a long moment, then slipped the phone back into his pocket without replying.



Elena was on the porch, coffee in hand, watching the late-morning sun burn the dew off the grass. She looked over at him, smiling, and he walked toward her — not because there wasn’t work to do, but because in this moment, he knew exactly where he needed to be.

Madison appeared in a flowy ivory blouse tucked into dark high-waisted trousers, oversized sunglasses perched on her head despite being indoors. Her note was short: “Heal. I’ll bring the champagne when you’re ready.”

Chapter 15 – Party Prep Night

By late afternoon the house had settled into a cheerful kind of chaos—the kind that smells like eucalyptus polish and peonies, that thrums with playlists drifting room to room, that makes even the quiet corners feel busy.



Sara and Harper had been there since morning, sleeves rolled, hair up, moving with the rhythm of people who know a space better than their own kitchens. Harper was coaxing taper candles into antique brass holders on the dining table while Sara circled back with a coach’s eye, nudging a vase two inches left, swapping a low bowl for a taller cluster of ranunculus. In the kitchen, trays of canapés lined up like a drill team. Tinsel-thin fairy lights tugged a soft glow across the beams.



Elena padded through it all with a list on her phone and that small, pleased smile she wore when home felt exactly right. Her emerald knit dress wrapped cleanly over the curve of her belly; a simple gold chain rested at her collarbone. Every few minutes she paused to sip sparkling water with lime and listen—Harper’s low whistle when a table turned out just so, Sara’s soft laugh, Grace’s slippers skimming the hardwood upstairs.



“Place cards done,” Harper called, setting a stack beside the china. “And if anyone asks, yes, I absolutely ironed the napkins. With love.”



Elena grinned. “I can’t believe you ironed napkins.”



“I can’t believe you trust Jasper with matches,” Harper shot back, then winked. “He’s banned from the candle table.”



“Noted,” Elena said, tapping her phone like she was filing it under policy.



Upstairs, the guest room had become a dressing studio: garment rack along the window, steamer hissing like a muted kettle, mirrors propped against the wall with ribbon-taped corners. Addison and Kendra had drawn the lucky duty of hemming and steaming and, in theory, keeping the chaos to a low simmer.



In practice, they started strong. Addison pinned a silk hem with quick, sure fingers while Kendra ran a careful pass of steam, the two of them trading tournament-style commentary.



“If this dress were a lift, she’s a clean and jerk,” Kendra said, eyes narrowed at a stubborn crease. “Explosive, then control.”



“Uh-huh,” Addison said. “And this seam is the part that makes me cry in the car after.”



They laughed. The room smelled faintly of lavender spray and hot fabric. Heat licked the windows.



When the last stubborn crease finally surrendered, they draped the silk on the chair back with something like reverence and—maybe because the room was warm, maybe because the day had been long and good, maybe because there’s a point where friendship leans into mischief—neither of them reached for the robes they’d left there.



“Victory lap?” Kendra teased, chin tipped, hair slid into a neat ponytail that showed off the clean line of her shoulders.



“Victory lap,” Addison said, and stepped in, hands light at Kendra’s jaw.



The kiss was unhurried and bright with laughter. When they broke apart, both bit their lower lips at the same time and then laughed harder at themselves, foreheads touching as if they were trying to catch their breath on the far side of a sprint.



“Ladies…”



They jolted. Elena leaned in the doorway, one hand around her glass, the other braced on the frame, amused as a cat in a sunspot. She took the scene in without hurry: the silk pooled like water on the chair back, the steamer sighing, the two culprits still close enough to count each other’s freckles.



“Finish your dresses before you start your after‑party,” she said, voice dry, eyes warm.



Addison and Kendra lunged, not gracefully, for the robes draped over the chair. Belts whispered fast through loops. Addison’s cheeks had the good sense to go pink; Kendra’s laugh tried to hide in her shoulder.



“And,” Elena added, sipping her lime, “make sure Grace doesn’t see it, unless you want a whole new set of questions.”



Small feet pattered down the hallway on cue. “Mom? Are they ready yet? I want to see the dresses!” Grace’s voice swung in, followed by another—brighter, older: “We’re helping!”



Chloe rounded the corner first, leggings tucked into socks, a constellation of glitter stickers peppering her cheek from an earlier craft. Grace barreled in behind her, hair ribbon askew, already halfway to the garment rack.



“We’re your assistants,” Chloe announced, hands on hips. “We require snacks.”



“Union rules,” Grace added solemnly.



Addison recovered fastest, kneeling to their height. “Good, because we’re hiring. Pay is hair clips and first pick of twirls.” She tapped Grace’s nose. “VIP privileges for you.”



Kendra scooped the steamer cord safely away from small feet. “And I’m promoting both of you to Chief Twirl Officers.”



“CTOs,” Chloe said, impressed. “That’s very professional.”



Elena shook her head, bemused, relief soft in her shoulders the way it had been since the hospital days. She crossed to the garment rack and lifted a blush tulle dress that caught the light like morning. “Alright, CTOs,” she said, “we have assignments. Grace, you’re with Addison on hair and sash. Chloe, you’re with Kendra on twirl physics.”



“Twirl physics,” Chloe repeated, awed. “Science.”



They moved like a small troupe: Addison gentle and deft with the ribbon at Grace’s waist, Kendra demonstrating skirt swoops with Chloe that turned into giggles and small, careful spins. Elena hovered just enough to be needed, hands tidying, eyes bright.



From downstairs, a new playlist eased into something a little slower. Sara’s voice carried up the stairwell: “Five-minute check on candles!”



“Coming,” Elena called, but she didn’t move yet. She watched the three of them for another beat—Addison smoothing Grace’s hair with serious concentration, Kendra crouched to Chloe’s level, grinning like a kid—and felt that sudden swell in her chest she’d learned not to apologize for.



Harper’s reflection appeared in the mirror, shoulder to the doorframe, eyebrow arched. “Everything decent?” she stage‑whispered.



“Barely,” Elena murmured, lips tipping. “But we’ve reached compliance.”



Harper snorted, then softened as she clocked the scene. “Alright, bosses,” she told the CTOs, clapping once, “finish up here and report downstairs for candle inspection.”



Chloe saluted. Grace twirled. The skirt fanned perfectly.



“Approved,” Kendra said, mock‑grave.



“Highly approved,” Addison added, kissing the top of Grace’s head. “Ten out of ten.”



Elena caught Harper’s eye in the mirror, something unspoken passing between them—gratitude, mischief, maybe a little warning about the robe incident they’d debrief later and laugh about forever.



“Okay,” Elena said, tucking a stray hair behind her ear, “downstairs. We’ve got lights to string and a front porch to charm.”



They filed out like a parade: Chloe marching with her chin up, Grace clutching Addison’s hand, Kendra balancing the steamer and a row of hair clips on her wrist like bangles, Harper scooping up a forgotten ribbon and looping it around Elena’s fingers as they went.



On the landing, Elena paused and looked back at the room—the garment rack, the mirror, the ordinary magic of a house on the verge of filling with people. Jasper would be home in an hour, hair still damp from a shower taken too fast, tie tugged straight as he walked through the door. The night would rush up to meet them.



For now, though, there were candles to light and a girl who needed to practice her twirl one more time. Elena smiled, set her glass on the banister, and followed the laughter down the stairs.

Book 2 – Chapter 1: Six Weeks Later

Setting: Late morning in D.C., Jasper’s office / Elena at home

Jasper is in his downtown office, jacket off, tie loosened, surrounded by three live conflicts from Book 1 still simmering — the NFL agent’s ongoing player scandal, the high-profile political clean-up in D.C., and the sports franchise ownership battle.



We see the NSA cyber guy briefing him quietly in the corner while Claire, newly brought in, sits on the edge of Jasper’s desk with a coffee, giving him a blunt pep talk about how much tension she’s still reading in the team.



Jasper checks his phone twice during the briefing — not because he’s distracted, but because Elena sent him a text of her and Grace at the CrossFit gym’s pool, Grace with swim goggles on, Elena in a navy two-piece athletic bikini that’s functional but still shows her new pregnancy curves. The image pulls a grin from him mid-sentence.



Cut to Elena

Elena’s morning is different now: she’s back working part-time in real estate and has started consulting for a non-profit three mornings a week.



Her style is noticeably shifted — Addison’s influence is everywhere. Today she’s wearing a cream silk blouse tucked into high-waisted, tailored navy trousers with gold-button detail, wedge espadrilles, and a thin gold chain necklace.



At the CrossFit gym earlier, she’d worn a fitted teal racerback tank and black compression leggings, hair in a high ponytail — Kendra had teased her about “owning the room” even before she got pregnant.

He won’t. But they both know the conversation has shifted since Book 1 — Elena isn’t waiting up frustrated anymore. She’s holding her space, and Jasper, even from a distance, respects it.

Chapter 2 — Salt Air, Tight Timelines

Sarasota, Florida — late afternoon



Jasper’s phone buzzed twice as the sedan rolled past palm rows toward the marina. Two different crises, same headache: the DC leak needed a follow‑up call, and the NFL cyber flags had doubled since breakfast. He slid the device face‑down on his thigh and looked out the window. Elena caught the move, smiled, and put her hand over his.



“Two hours,” she said. “We can give Harper two hours without you solving America.”



He exhaled a laugh. “Sixty minutes to triage, sixty for charm. I’ll try.”



Elena had dressed for Florida like she owned the horizon—white silk shell, coral wrap skirt, gold hoops, simple sandals. The air-con raised a soft gooseflesh on her arms, and he reached to smooth it with his thumb. Six weeks into showing, and she had found a stride that looked like joy.



Harper waved them down from the boardwalk—sunburned shoulders, a linen dress that caught the wind, the bright, clipped energy of someone running at too many speeds at once. The man beside her stood in that easy, efficient way the military puts into a body: back straight, jaw relaxed, eyes always measuring.



“J/E!” Harper pulled Elena into a hug and rose to her toes to peck Jasper’s cheek. “You made it.”



“Wouldn’t miss a negotiation disguised as dinner,” Jasper said, offering his hand to the boyfriend. “Jasper Barrett.”



“Evan Hale,” the man said, firm grip, no show. “Thanks for meeting us on short notice.”



The hostess led them to a corner table with a view of the slips and a band warming up on steel drums. Elena ordered sparkling water with lime; Jasper, an iced tea; Harper and Evan split whatever local lager the waiter recommended.



Conversation did the polite circuit first—travel, weather, Florida drivers—and then landed where it always does when a strategist meets a soldier.



“You on the same base long?” Jasper asked.



“Mostly forward,” Evan said. It was an answer and a boundary.



Elena nudged it open with a grin. “Translation for civilians?”



“Rotations,” Evan said, eyes softening as he glanced at Harper. “It’s fine. We make it work.”



Harper’s fingers tucked into his like it was a reflex. “He’s better at time zones than I am.”



Jasper let the silence hang for a beat. He’d learned you can hear a lot in what people don’t fill. Evan’s watch was dinged stainless, not a showpiece. His shoes were polished, but salt‑scuffed. He clocked exits without looking obvious. Professional competence, high. Performative nonsense, low. Useful.



The waiter set down grouper tacos and a mountain of citrus slaw. They ate; the band found its groove.



Harper pivoted to work, clearly trying to preempt the lecture. “I’m back in Charlotte tomorrow. Contract comms for the CrossFit sponsor are queued. I left Addison the sheet.”



“Addison’s sheet,” Jasper said mildly, “or yours?”



Harper’s smile faltered a fraction. “Shared sheet.”



Elena bailed her out with a simple nod. “We’ll look it over tonight. Easy fix if anything’s double‑booked.”



Across the table, Evan took that in without comment. Jasper liked that, too. Men who didn’t meddle were rare and valuable.



Phones face‑down became a rule by silent consent. They ate key lime pie they hadn’t planned on. Elena asked Evan about music; he confessed to a guilty‑pleasure country playlist; Harper hazed him for it and then sang a chorus under her breath. For a pocket of time, the world was four people and a Gulf sunset.



When the check came, Evan reached, and Jasper let him have it. Another quiet test passed.



On the boardwalk afterward, the marina lights came up like a runway. Harper tugged Elena aside for a girl‑huddle; Jasper and Evan drifted to the rail.



“She’s good at what she does,” Evan said, watching the water. “But the pace eats her.”



“She picked a profession that turns adrenaline into currency,” Jasper said. “We teach the better ones how not to spend it all in one place.”



“That a pitch?”



“A warning,” Jasper said, then softened it. “And an offer. When she stumbles—and everyone does—there are people there to catch her.”



Evan nodded once. “Good.”



Behind them, Elena squeezed Harper’s hands. “We like him,” she whispered.



“You sure?” Harper’s eyes were bright, a little defiant, a little hopeful. “Jasper’s doing the… Jasper thing.”



“He’s doing the protector thing,” Elena said. “Let him. It’s how he loves us.”



Harper breathed out. “Okay.”



They parted under string lights, promises of breakfast they all knew would be broken by flights and blowups.



In the car, Jasper’s phone face‑up was a crime scene: six missed calls, two “urgent” tags, one text from Addison that read Courier window moved 90 minutes. I’ve got it. Kendra had added, I can cover athlete touchpoints. Go be human.



Elena watched his thumb hover. “Two hours,” she repeated. “We did ninety minutes. I can be generous.”



He smiled without looking at the screen. “You already are.”



He called Addison first, then the NSA contact. By the time they reached the hotel, the outlines of a plan had reassembled themselves around the evening.



Elena slipped her arm through his as they crossed the lobby. “So?”



“He’s competent,” Jasper said. “And he knows what he doesn’t say.”



“That’s a yes with an asterisk.”



“It’s a yes that wants more data,” he said, and kissed her temple in the elevator. “How’s my data set doing?”



She leaned into him, voice low. “Your data set made friends, ate pie, and still has room for breakfast.”



“Breakfast,” he repeated, like a promise.



Charlotte — the next morning



Addison met Kendra at the office espresso machine in a dress that could pass for a power suit if you squinted—ink‑blue sheath, hair up, phone in one hand and a highlighter in the other. Kendra had a “don’t kill me” smile and a stack of color‑coded schedules.



“Tell me you didn’t double‑book the courier,” Addison said, without looking up.



“I moved the courier,” Kendra said. “And I roughed out athlete comms for the next 48 hours. If Harper needs… breathing room.”



Addison’s glance flicked up, appreciative. “You’re learning the calculus.”



Kendra shrugged. “You run at six speeds. I’m just trying to keep up.”



“You keep up fine,” Addison said, and then—softer—“Thanks.”



Harper walked in a beat later, sunlit, ponytail high, eyes on her phone. She stopped when she saw the stack waiting for her. Shame and relief did a quick, quiet war on her face.



“I’ll make the calls,” she said.



“You’ll make the calls,” Addison agreed, sliding over a pen. “And we’re good.”



DC — that afternoon



Jasper found a pocket park, sat on the warm stone edge of a fountain, and called Elena. She picked up on the first ring; he could hear gulls in the background, even though she was nowhere near the coast.



“How was breakfast?” he asked.



“A lie, as foretold,” she said. “Airport bagel. But Harper texted; they’re on their way. And I signed a listing.”



“That’s my girl.” He let the pride show; she earned every watt of it.



“And your boy?”



He glanced down at the bulleted list he’d made on a napkin. “Wants to be a man who gets home for dinner.”



“Ambitious,” she teased. “We’ll settle for FaceTime. Seven?”



“Seven,” he said. “And I’ll wear a tie.”



She laughed. “Do that, and I’ll change into something that matches.”



He hung up, looked at the napkin again, and added a line he’d been avoiding:



Delegate or drown.



A breeze rolled through the square. For a second—long enough to count—Jasper Barrett allowed the world to turn without him forcing it. Then he stood, slid the phone into his pocket, and went back to making sure the fires burned where they were supposed to, and not where they weren’t.

Elena met Sara and Addison at a boutique that believed in mirrors and merciless lighting. Sara had already pulled four dresses, all color and shape.



“Try the magenta,” Sara commanded, handing it over like a prescription.

Sara nodded once, satisfied. “Buy it. Wear it. End scene.”

“Yes?”



“Yes. Wear it. Then lock the door.”



She rolled her eyes, delighted. “Go triage your disasters.”

“Good.” She hesitated. “How’s the fourth conflict?”



“The memoir?” He smirked. “If they spell my name right, it’s marketing.”

D.C. — early afternoon



Jasper took the FaceTime with Addison from the back of the car. She had three tabs open, one earbud in, and hair up in a knot that meant I’m running the room even if I’m alone in it.



“Hold lines loaded,” she said, flicking a document his way. “I’m also pre‑drafting the mea culpa that isn’t a mea culpa if the rumor turns out partially true. We can shape this as ‘values alignment’ with a charity pivot. The athlete’s foundation is squeaky clean—let’s widen that.”

Addison’s eyes lit. “Already pinged her.”

Jasper looked out the window, jaw a slow set. “I know. We’ll coach, not crush.”

“If the author wants attention, starving them is the move. We go quiet and build better noise.” He glanced down at the other alert. “How’s our tech patient?”

Charlotte — midday



Elena swung by the office to sign a listing agreement, then headed to the CrossFit gym, the magenta dress now tucked into a garment bag in the passenger seat like contraband. She changed into black leggings and a cobalt tank, tied her hair up, and stepped onto the floor just as the noon class broke.



Kendra was at the whiteboard, writing split times in tidy block letters. Up close she was all geometry—long lines, calm presence, eyes that measured and then encouraged.



“You’re Elena,” Kendra said, offering a chalk-dusted hand. “I’ve heard six different stories about your barbell PR and none of them match.”



Elena laughed. “All of them are lies, but I won’t correct the flattering ones.”

Her gaze flicked, not unkindly, to Elena’s midsection. Elena liked her instantly for the respect in that look.



“Swim,” Elena said. “Then pulls. I’m auditioning for ‘competent.’”

Kendra shook her head, amused, and reset the clock. “Three, two—go.”



Elena slipped into the pool after the set, letting the cool water quiet the chatter in her head. On the fourth lap, she reached the wall, popped up, and found Addison leaning on the edge, chin on folded arms.



“You good?” Addison asked.



Elena blew a strand of hair from her face. “Pregnant, magenta, and mildly terrified. You?”



“Single, overcaffeinated, and about to save Jasper from a PR migraine.” She tilted her head. “Harper?”



“White‑knuckling,” Elena said. “Backstop quiet, yeah?”



“Always.”



They pushed off the wall together, two clean lines through water.



D.C. — late afternoon



The meeting with the tech founder who had ghosted his media plan happened in a glass box with a view of a river that had seen worse. Jasper let the man talk for seven minutes—excuses, “timing,” “bandwidth,” all the greatest hits—then he slid a single page across the table.



“This is your timeline,” he said. “This is your funding runway. This is the day you lose your investor if we don’t move inside 72 hours. Now, tell me again about bandwidth.”



Silence did its work. At minute nine, the founder exhaled. “What do you need?”



“Commitment and a camera,” Jasper said. “We’ll build the rest.”



When he walked out, his phone vibrated with a message from Marcus: Bishop. Call on secure.



He ducked into a courtyard and hit the line. Marcus’s voice was the same dry gravel that had talked him through three other breaches and one near-coup far from here.



“We’ve contained the active exfil,” Marcus said. “But there’s a copy floating. We seeded a better one. If press bites, they bite our version.”



“Good,” Jasper said. “Anyone we need to protect first?”



“Your client’s GC. She’s competent. She’ll be fine if you give her three talking points and a spine.”



“I’ll loan her mine,” Jasper said. “Anything else?”



Marcus hesitated. “Tell your Florida friend to watch her inbox. She missed a ping yesterday she shouldn’t have.”



Jasper’s pause was a fraction too long. “Noted.”



He ended the call and looked up at the slice of sky between buildings. Delegate or drown, he’d written on a napkin. Time to walk it.



He dialed Harper. Voicemail. He texted instead: Call me when you land. And check your security filters. Today.



Then he called Elena.



Charlotte — early evening



Elena answered on the second ring, the sounds of home behind her—water running, the clink of a pan, Grace’s voice somewhere down the hall narrating a stuffed animal rescue.



“Tell me something good,” she said.

“She needs sleep and a second set of eyes,” he said. “I’m putting Addison under her for a week. Quietly.”



“Good.” Elena tasted sauce, frowned, added salt. “I met Kendra. I like her.”



“You would,” he said. “She reads a room like she reads a bar path.”



Elena smiled at the stove. “Also, I bought a dress that might restart your heart.”



“I already died once today,” he said. “I’ll risk it.”



“FaceTime at seven?” she asked.



“Seven,” he said. “Tie optional?”



“Not optional,” she said, and he could hear the grin.



He hung up and, for the second time that day, let the world turn for a breath without him pushing. Then he picked up the next instrument and went back to work.

Announcement Party – Full Scene Narrative

The great room of the rental in the mountains glowed with golden afternoon light, fire flickering in the stone hearth. Outside, the Blue Ridge shimmered in the distance, peaks softened by the lingering winter haze. Inside, Elena had arranged a long farmhouse table groaning under platters of smoked meats, roasted vegetables, artisan bread, and a towering cake covered in pale ivory fondant.



Elena, in a deep forest-green wrap dress that skimmed her still-slim frame, her dark hair twisted into a loose low chignon, was doing her best to stay seated on the wide linen sofa. Addie—black jumpsuit, hair in a high, sharp ponytail—was perched on the arm next to her, serving as unofficial bodyguard, making sure Elena didn’t overdo it.



Kendra, in a cream cable-knit sweater and dark jeans tucked into knee-high brown boots, was across the room at the charcuterie table chatting with Savannah (flowy burgundy maxi dress, gold hoop earrings) and two of the newer wives club members:



Dani Wells – Blonde pixie cut, icy blue eyes, sharp humor. Married to Nate Wells, a cybersecurity consultant who’d recently joined Jasper’s extended professional circle. Dani ran her own boutique travel concierge firm and was known for turning even simple girls’ weekends into five-star experiences.



Madison Clarke – Chestnut waves, warm brown eyes, always the social butterfly. Married to Evan Clarke, a venture capital partner. Madison co-owned a fitness and lifestyle brand and could make friends with anyone within five minutes.



Isabel Romero – Elegant and understated, dark hair to her waist, married to Miguel Romero, a high-end architect. Isabel ran a nonprofit focused on literacy programs for underserved kids.



Grace was darting between legs in a blush tulle dress and glitter sneakers, giggling with a juice box in hand. Every few minutes, Elena’s eyes flicked to the front door. Jasper had texted thirty minutes ago: On my way. Cutting it close.



The sound of the front door swinging open cut through the low hum of conversation. Cold mountain air swept in, and there he was—Jasper—wearing a navy suit, jacket slung over his forearm, tie loosened, a touch of wind in his hair from the dash from the car. His eyes immediately found Elena, and before he could even set down his briefcase, Grace squealed, “Daddy!” and raced toward him.



He caught her mid-run, lifting her up with one arm and kissing her cheek before crossing the room in a straight line to Elena. He leaned down, kissing her softly, his hand cupping her cheek.



“Sorry I’m late,” he murmured, eyes warm. “Calls wouldn’t end. You look incredible.”



“You made it,” she replied, relief in her voice.

Elena reached for the white box on the coffee table, lifting the lid to reveal a tiny, neatly folded blue onesie with the words Future MVP embroidered in silver thread.



There was a beat of silence before the room erupted—cheers, applause, a few happy tears from Savannah, and Madison exclaiming, “I knew it was a boy!” Dani was already pulling her phone to snap a discreet photo. Isabel smiled gently, leaning in to hug Elena.



The men in the room—Nate Wells, Evan Clarke, Miguel Romero, and a few of Jasper’s old friends from Charlotte—offered Jasper back slaps and quick congratulations, though the conversation quickly turned to sports and the best bourbon in the house.

The sun rose bright and warm over the beach rental, light spilling across the ocean and into the wide windows. Downstairs, the smell of coffee drifted up, but upstairs, the master bedroom was a bustling prep zone.



Addie stood barefoot by the garment rack, robe loosely tied over a blush silk bra and panties, steam curling from the wand in her hand. She hummed softly as she coaxed the last wrinkle out of a flowing chiffon bridesmaid dress.



The bathroom door cracked open and Kendra emerged, hair damp, robe hanging open over a deep emerald lace set. She paused, taking in the scene with a crooked smile.

“Looks like a boutique exploded in here.”



Addie didn’t look up. “Better than having wrinkles immortalized in wedding photos. Grab the other steamer before I die in here.”



They worked side by side, trading dresses, leaning past one another, their robes shifting and brushing. The air was warm and charged, each accidental touch lingering longer than it needed to.



When Kendra reached past to hang a dress, her robe slipped wider, revealing a flat stomach and the hint of lace. Addie caught herself staring.

“You always dress like this for work, or am I just lucky today?”



“Maybe I like the company,” Kendra replied, eyes holding hers for a beat longer than usual.



The moment was broken when the door swung open. Elena stood there, coffee in hand, eyebrows arched.

“Well,” she said slowly, “I don’t think I need to ask how much fun you two are having without me.”



Addie grinned. “Just making sure your dresses look perfect.”

Kendra added, “And maybe making sure she doesn’t burn herself.”



Elena shook her head, smirking as she walked off. “Uh-huh. Save some of that energy for the reception.”



Both women laughed — but neither denied the charge hanging between them.



Hair & Makeup

By midmorning, the upstairs was a hum of blow dryers, curling irons, and makeup brushes. The bridal party bustled in and out, champagne flutes in hand. Grace made her rounds with a tiny basket of snacks, occasionally darting under the garment rack to “help.”



Ceremony

The beach ceremony was stunning — sunset-gold light pouring over white chairs and florals. Elena held Grace on her lap during the vows, watching with that mix of pride and wistfulness she always carried at weddings. Jasper had sent flowers from DC, the card tucked into her clutch.



Reception

As the music turned from elegant dinner tunes to a lively dance floor mix, the champagne flowed freely. Addie and Kendra found themselves paired for a slow song, laughing as they tried to match steps.



The Kiss

Later, in the shadowed hallway off the main reception room, Addie leaned against the wall, breathless from dancing. Kendra slipped in beside her, cheeks flushed.

“Guess we clean up nice,” Kendra said softly.



Addie’s gaze flicked to her lips before she could stop herself. “Yeah. We really do.”



There was no buildup — Kendra closed the gap, their mouths meeting in a kiss that started playful and deepened until the music from the next room blurred into the background.



When they broke apart, both were a little breathless. Addie gave a wry smile. “That… was unexpected.”

Kendra smirked. “Was it?”



Before they could say more, the sound of footsteps made them pull apart. They smoothed their dresses and walked back toward the party, unspoken electricity still running between them.

Jasper sat beside her, one hand on her shoulder, the other gently stroking Grace’s hair as she stared wide-eyed at her baby brother.



The first wave of visitors trickled in: Sara with her husband and kids, Jessica with flowers, and even Harper arriving late from the airport still in travel clothes. The room filled with chatter, congratulations, and laughter. Nurses bustled in and out, but no one seemed to notice—this was family.



Addie and Kendra hung back, protective shadows near the corner of the room. Both had puffy eyes from emotion, but they carried themselves like sentries, making sure nothing disturbed Elena or the baby.



Quiet Moment: Addie & Elena

Later, after visitors thinned, Addie slipped to Elena’s bedside while Jasper took Grace for a snack downstairs. Elena studied her face immediately, motherly intuition sharp.



Addie swallowed hard. “He’s perfect. And you… you’re incredible.”



Elena smiled, tired but glowing. “Thank you for everything, Addie. Really. You’ve carried more than I could ever ask this year.”



Addie shifted, voice trembling. “I don’t… I don’t want to give you up. Or this. Being part of this family—it’s the most real thing I’ve ever known.”



Elena reached out, brushing Addie’s cheek. “You don’t have to give it up. We’ll figure this out. Together.”



Addie’s tears finally broke, and she leaned in, forehead resting gently against Elena’s.



Quiet Moment: Kendra & Elena

Later that night, after Grace fell asleep curled in a chair, Kendra found her own moment. Elena was nursing Lucas when Kendra approached.



“You’re a rockstar,” Kendra whispered, leaning against the wall.



Elena smirked tiredly. “You’re not so bad yourself. Addie told me how much you’ve held it together.”



Kendra hesitated, then admitted, “I love her. In ways I didn’t think I could. But I know it’s… complicated.”



Elena’s gaze softened. “Then we’ll talk. Not now, not here—but when I’m home. All of us. No secrets. No shame.”



Kendra nodded, relief loosening her chest. “Deal.”



Jasper Pulled Away

By Thursday morning, the hospital room was calmer. Visitors came in waves, the wives’ club filtering through with casseroles, balloons, and advice. The newest wives—Rachel, Kim, and Sophia—arrived together, all eager smiles and nervous energy, quickly welcomed into the fold.



But Jasper’s phone never stopped buzzing. Finally, he kissed Elena’s forehead, whispered something that made her smile, and slipped out the door in a pressed shirt and jacket. Another fire to put out.



Addie watched him go, torn between admiration and worry. Kendra caught her glance, the two of them reading each other’s thoughts without words.



Closing Beat

As night fell, Elena rocked Lucas in her arms, Grace asleep beside her, and two loyal shadows—Addie and Kendra—on the couch, whispering about duty, love, and what came next.



And Elena, half-dreaming, thought: When I get home… we’ll all sit down. Together. And finally talk about what we’ve started.



Meanwhile, Jasper’s car pulled into the office garage. The last scenario of this book awaited.

Grace

Grace insisted on a glittery blue tulle dress, silver headband, and a small plastic tiara Addie had given her earlier in the week. She marched in holding Elena’s hand, then immediately ran toward the lights, declaring herself “party princess.”



Ridge & Marissa

Ridge looked surprisingly polished — dark navy blazer, fitted jeans, and polished brown boots. He wasn’t usually a “party guy,” but Marissa had worked magic.

Harper

Kendra

Sara & Jessica

Jessica wore a deep plum dress with matching lipstick, her heels clicking as she made her way across the stone patio. Always put together, always commanding.

📖 Book 1 — Circles of Fire

A story of family, loyalty, and the fragile balance between war abroad and peace at home.



Jasper Barrett is a fixer in Washington, D.C., pulled into conflicts where every call could decide the fate of nations. But when his wife Elena spirals after giving birth, the true fight moves closer to home.



His sister Addie steps in, carrying the weight of the household—managing crises, soothing Elena’s collapse, and protecting Grace, the daughter who only sees her mother as a hero. Kendra, fierce and loyal, joins Addie in holding the family together, blurring lines with her teasing affection and her own complicated romance with Ethan, a man of faith torn between patience and desire.



As DC burns with conflict, the Barrett household becomes its own battlefield of recovery, temptation, and love. Circles of Fire is where healing begins, where trust is tested, and where bonds between sisters, lovers, and family prove stronger than war.



📖 Book 2 — Threads of Ashes

Every victory costs something. Every secret carries weight.



The Barrett circle seems to steady—Elena finds her way back, Addie anchors the home, Kendra juggles desire and devotion—but new sparks ignite from old embers. A Midwest thread of crisis drags Jasper deeper into shadow wars. Addie, flirty but brilliant, finds herself shouldering the mantle of leadership while teasingly tangling with Kendra in games of intimacy and trust.



Ethan enters deeper into the family’s orbit, a faithful Catholic pulled between patience and passion, while Daniel—a new fixer with a PhD, five languages, and no military past—emerges as Jasper’s sharpest new weapon, and possibly Addie’s greatest temptation.



Between the playful heat of secret bids, trophy games, and flirtation, and the cold steel of geopolitical fallout, the Barretts must navigate what it means to love, to wait, and to fight. Threads of Ashes is where family ties and national conflicts collide—where love becomes strategy, and strategy becomes survival.

Where did wonder woman come from 

ChatGPT said:



Wonder Woman was created in the early 1940s by William Moulton Marston (a psychologist, inventor, and writer) and artist H.G. Peter.



She first appeared in All Star Comics #8 (December 1941) and then starred in Sensation Comics #1 (January 1942).



Her backstory drew on Greek mythology — she was Princess Diana of Themyscira, an Amazon warrior trained to be the world’s greatest fighter.



Her character was created as both a feminist icon and a counterbalance to the flood of male superheroes like Superman and Batman. Marston’s wife, Elizabeth, and their partner, Olive Byrne, heavily inspired Wonder Woman’s design and personality.



That ties neatly to your earlier pick for Athena Ascent CrossFit — Wonder Woman was often portrayed as a champion of strength, wisdom, and justice, almost like a modern embodiment of Athena.

✦ Scene 2: Redirecting to a Bigger Play

Yes — Olympic rowing has both singles and team events, which is part of what makes it such a versatile sport for character building. Here’s the breakdown:



🚣 Olympic Rowing Events (simplified):

Singles (1 person per boat)



Single Sculls (1x) → one rower with two oars.



Very physically demanding, often seen as the ultimate test of individual endurance, grit, and mental toughness.



Doubles / Pairs (2 people per boat)



Double Sculls (2x) → two rowers, each with two oars.



Pairs (2-) → two rowers, each with one oar, no coxswain.



Fours (4 people per boat)



Quadruple Sculls (4x) → four rowers, two oars each.



Four (4-) → four rowers, one oar each, no coxswain.



Eights (8+)



Eight rowers, one oar each, with a coxswain steering and coordinating.



The prestige, powerhouse event — lots of tradition, especially in the Ivy League and British rowing cultures.



🎭 For Sabrina Bloomfield

If you want her to embody independence and raw grit → make her a Single Sculls rower (brutal, lonely, pure endurance).



If you want her tied into team dynamics, camaraderie, and elite networks → make her part of the Eights (lots of Ivy/old-money connections here, think Henley Regatta).



She could even have a history of switching: competed in Singles for personal glory, then in Eights for Olympic medals.

Jasper Barrett – 8 Flashbacks

Duke Lacrosse Tryout (Freshman Year)

POV: Jasper

The whistle shrieked, sweat already slicking his palms. The older guys laughed when they saw him — a lanky freshman from a working-class family, not the polished prep kids they were used to. You don’t belong here, a voice whispered in his head. Then the first face-off whistle blew. He charged, dug into the turf, and sent the ball flying. By the end of practice, one senior slapped him on the back. “You’re scrappy, Barrett. I like that.”



Late Nights with Dad’s Toolbelt

He watched his father at the kitchen table, dirt under his nails, sorting through old bolts and screws. Jasper handed him a wrench that was too big. His dad just grinned: “Wrong size, son, but I like that you tried. Keep looking. You’ll figure it out.” Jasper tucked that lesson away — fix what’s in front of you, even if it takes a few wrong tries.



First Big Save – Construction Site

At 23, standing on scaffolding above a faltering project in Charlotte, he caught the error no one else saw: the load-bearing beams ordered in the wrong size. He made the call, rerouted suppliers, and kept the building upright. Jessica Vaughn noticed. “You kept this thing from collapsing,” she told him. “Ever think about fixing bigger problems?”



Meeting Jessica for the First Time

Her office looked like a command center. She asked him one question: “Do you want to manage, or do you want to lead?” He swallowed hard. “Lead.” She smiled. “Then you’ll do.” That was the beginning of BSS.



First Party at Oak Watch

He’d never seen so many tuxedos in one place. Senators, investors, even an NFL owner sipping bourbon by the fire. He hovered by the bar until Mason shoved a glass into his hand. “Relax, brother. They bleed like the rest of us.”



Meeting Elena Again (after the 3-year break)

2. The Range Rules

During one of Addie and Hawk’s range dates, Grace insists on coming along. She’s outfitted in oversized earmuffs, safety glasses, and a pink backpack full of snacks.

3. Postpartum Protector

When Elena is still in her fragile postpartum stage, Grace climbs onto the bed with her mom, curling against her side.

4. Fashion Judge

5. Game Night Chaos

“Never have I ever… kissed anyone. Except Mommy. And Daddy. And Aunt Addie. And Aunt Kendra. And Uncle Hawk. Okay maybe I kissed everyone.”



The room erupts. Addie nearly spits out her drink. Kendra hides her laugh in a pillow. Jasper mutters: “She’s already running this house.”



6. The Swim Coach

At the pool, Grace insists on coaching Kendra during laps. She paces the side of the pool with a whistle she got from Sara’s gym.



“Kick harder! No slacking, Aunt Kendra! Faster, faster! Aunt Addie’s beating you!”



When Kendra climbs out, Grace hands her a juice box like it’s a medal. “Good race. But you lost. We’ll train tomorrow.”



Addie smirks, whispering, “See? She’s scarier than Lexi with a deadline.”



7. First Sleepover at Emberhearth

One night, Grace begs to sleep over at Addie’s place. She shows up with a stuffed unicorn, a toothbrush, and Frozen 2 on Blu-ray.

During bedtime, she snuggles between Addie and Kendra and announces:



“This is way better than a hotel. You two are like my other moms.”



Addie and Kendra exchange a glance — half flustered, half touched. Grace is already asleep before either of them can respond.



8. Mini-Strategist
